title: What is the right way of assessing AI?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou takes the stream of reports that large language models ace legal, medical and other exams and argues that, by the standards of assessment theory, those scores are close to meaningless. The foundational principle, quoting Daniel Koretz, is that a test score is only a small sample of behaviour and matters only for the inferences it supports. Cheating, test prep and confounds such as word-heavy maths questions all weaken those inferences for humans, and the same standard should apply to AI, especially as we do not know how models pass, and test answers may sit in their training data. She answers the charge of moving the goalposts by saying this principle has underpinned assessment for decades. As a better benchmark she proposes a probationary-period style evaluation of actual job performance, where some AI does well and others, like ChatGPT assessing writing, do not.
points: A test score is meaningless by itself; what matters is which inferences an end-user can legitimately draw from it.
Applying the same standard to AI, passing professional exams says little, particularly when training data may include the tests and answers.
Misunderstanding the inference principle has led policymakers astray and fuelled bad test prep that teaches to the sampled content.
Christodoulou rejects the goalpost-moving charge because the principle of validity applies equally to human test-takers.
A probationary-period approach to evaluating AI at real work is more direct and avoids complex validation questions.
quotes: This might seem so obvious it is barely worth mentioning, but it gets to the heart of one of the most fundamental principles of assessment - which is that the test score by itself is totally meaningless. What matters are the inferences that you can make from this test score.
It doesn't matter if you get every question right. It doesn't matter if you get every question wrong. What matters are the inferences that an end-user can make about those results.
If a student does poorly on a maths exam with lots of word questions, can you infer they are bad at maths, or only that they are bad at language?

If we are apply the same standard to AI, then the fact that it is acing exams is essentially meaningless. In order to validate its results, we need to know more about how they are achieved and therefore what inferences the results allow us to support or not.

AI researchers have rushed to write peer-reviewed articles about how LLMs passing exams is a watershed moment of huge significance - without even bothering to do the most basic research on what those exams are and what they can and cannot tell you.

But I hope you can see that in this case, I am absolutely not moving the goalposts. The goalpost in question here is a principle that forms the fundamental basis of all assessment, and has done for decades. And it's a goalpost that I would apply equally to a human test-taker.
